metadata.title: How AI Draws Anime Frames
metadata.visual_policy: Simple illustrative shapes only. No frames or characters from Naruto or any real anime.

beats.narration_text: Fans often say AI-smoothed anime looks unnatural. Yet in 2025, Toei, the studio behind One Piece, said it expects to use AI to draw in-between frames. So if AI drew your favourite anime on its own, would you still love it the same way?

shot.visual_intent: Two identical shapes move side by side, hand-timed versus smoothed; the question is the last thing on screen.

show.event: two copies of one abstract shape cross the frame: left steps in held drawings, right glides
'unnatural' lands as a label on the gliding side
a small sourced line appears: 'AI for in-between frames (Anime Corner, 2025)'; empty slots between two drawings fill in

the shapes clear and the closing question is left on screen: 'If AI drew your favourite anime on its own,' arrives with a dashed empty slot beneath it, and 'would you still love it the same way?' lands inside the slot

beats.narration_text: AI can be the animator's helping hand. It can draw the in-betweens, but only the animator decides the timing. Let's see why.

beats.narration_text: Anime is hand-drawn animation, and every scene starts with key frames. A key animator draws the most important poses, like Rock Lee launching his kick at Gaara, and the moment it lands. Then in-between artists draw the frames that connect them. Those in-betweens are exactly the drawings AI is being asked to make.

shot.visual_intent: Two key poses of a plain capsule and a target block, then the drawings that connect them.

show.event: an empty timeline with two thick key-frame cells
key pose 1: a capsule pulls back, labelled 'launch'
key pose 2: the capsule reaches a block, labelled 'lands'
pale in-between drawings fill the gap one at a time along the arc
the in-betweens take the accent colour under the label 'what AI is asked to draw'

beats.narration_text: Video plays at twenty-four frames a second, but anime rarely draws all twenty-four. Most of it is drawn on twos or threes: each drawing is held for two or three frames, so just twelve or eight drawings a second. Fast action, like a punch, can be drawn on ones. These holds are a choice, about budget and about feel.

shot.visual_intent: One 24-cell strip for one second of video; holds regroup it in step with the narration.

show.event: a strip of 24 cells labelled '24 frames = one second'; 'anime rarely draws all 24' follows
the strip moves up and recolours into pairs under 'on twos'; a second strip recolours into threes under 'on threes'; an empty outline of a third strip waits below
a marker sweeps across each row, hanging longer on threes
the labels complete as 'on twos: 12 drawings' and 'on threes: just 8'
the empty outline fills as a third strip, which then recolours under 'on ones: all 24' and its marker moves fast
'a choice about budget and feel' lands beneath the three strips

beats.narration_text: So how does AI make a new frame? First it calculates optical flow: a map of arrows showing where each pixel moved from one frame to the next. Then it follows those arrows halfway and draws the frame in the middle. On live-action video, full of texture and small movements, this works surprisingly well.

shot.visual_intent: The mechanism performs itself on a textured dot field.

show.event: frame A and frame B side by side, each a speckled texture with a shape shifted between them
arrows grow from A to B across the field, labelled 'optical flow'
dots travel halfway along the arrows into an empty middle frame, which fills in
the finished three frames hold with a check mark and 'lots of texture to track'

qc.contrast_reason: The arrows and dots are drawings, not type; text checks apply to the frame labels and caption.
qc.typography_reason: The arrows and dots are drawings, not type; text checks apply to the frame labels and caption.

beats.narration_text: Anime breaks it in three ways. Flat colors: a sleeve painted one solid color has no texture, so the AI can't tell which pixel went where. Big movement: think of Naruto and Sasuke's final fight. Between two drawings, a fist can fly halfway across the screen along a curve. And hidden parts: a hand that slips behind the body has nothing to match. The result is ghosting, blur, even extra limbs.

shot.visual_intent: Three panels built one by one, each failing visibly, ending on the failures in the interpolated frame.

show.event: three empty panels: 'flat colors', 'big movement', 'hidden parts'
flat colors: a one-colour rectangle sleeve shifts; arrows scatter randomly with question marks
big movement: a circle jumps most of the panel along a curve; a straight flow guess misses it
hidden parts: a circle slides behind a block; its match line ends in 'no match'
one abstract shape shows the results in turn: 'ghosting', 'blur', 'extra limbs'

beats.narration_text: That's why many fans and animators dislike 60 fps AI edits. Smoothing every frame wipes out the timing the animator chose. One critic called the result lifeless. As a fan, I agree. A little AI here and there is fine, but a whole anime smoothed this way looks unnatural to me.

shot.visual_intent: Timing strip with chosen holds is flattened into even ticks; contrast held side by side.

show.event: an uneven strip of held drawings labelled 'the animator's timing'
even 60 fps ticks sweep across a copy and flatten its holds; label: 'every frame smoothed'
quote card: 'lifeless', credited to The A.V. Club
both strips hold side by side; a small 'a little AI' tick stays, a whole strip is marked 'unnatural to me'

beats.narration_text: Researchers are now building AI for anime itself. One 2021 project, AnimeInterp, built a dataset of twelve thousand sets of anime frames, and its model matches the flat color shapes between two drawings before it guesses the motion. Tools like this could take repetitive in-betweens off an animator's desk, with the animator still checking every frame.

shot.visual_intent: Two simple drawings made of flat colour regions; regions are paired before motion is estimated.

show.event: two simple drawings built from flat colour regions
a counter runs to 12,000 labelled 'sets of anime frames (AnimeInterp, 2021)'
matching regions link across the two drawings, colour to colour
motion arrows appear only after the regions are linked
a stack of in-betweens leaves a desk shape; every frame passes a pencil and a check mark under 'animator checks'

beats.narration_text: So, can AI draw anime frames? It can draw the in-betweens. But it struggles with flat colors, big movement and hidden parts, and it can't choose the timing. That choice is where the feeling lives. AI should be the animator's helping hand, not their replacement.

show.event: the one-page card opens on the question
the first line lands
the three struggles land
the timing line lands
the helping-hand line closes the page

artifactLines: It struggles with flat colors, big movement and hidden parts.
The animator's helping hand, not their replacement.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: I'm an anime fan, not an animator. Using a scene from my favourite anime, explain like I'm twelve how an animator decides which drawings to make and how long to hold each one. Then tell me which parts AI could safely help with, and which should stay hand-drawn. And next time an animation amazes you, look up how it was made, frame by frame. You'll never watch it the same way.

the prompt holds, ready to copy, while the closing invitation is spoken
